summary: States the requirements for converting a permanent connection into a soft permanent connection, and the reverse, in a GMPLS network without disturbing the traffic it carries. From a carrier viewpoint, this changes who owns and controls the connection.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone company has lines set up by hand and lines set up by software. This note lists what is needed to switch a line from one kind to the other while people are still using it.

subtitle: Converting connections between operator control and automatic control without disrupting traffic.

tldr.problem: Transport networks have connections owned by either the management plane (set up by operators) or the control plane (set up by automated protocols), but migrating existing traffic from one to the other is difficult without interruption.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines requirements for converting between permanent connections (management-owned), switched connections (control-owned), and soft permanent connections (hybrid), while keeping data flowing without gaps or alarms.
tldr.outcome: Carriers can gradually shift control of an existing network from manual provisioning to automated GMPLS, and roll back if needed, without downtime.

facts.label: Primary use case
facts.value: Network migration from NMS to GMPLS

today: RFC 5493 is an Informational document that remains current. It provides the requirements foundation for GMPLS-based network evolution, supporting carriers in introducing control plane automation into existing management-plane-provisioned networks.

sections.title: Permanent and Switched Connections
sections.content:
In transport networks, a data plane connection between two endpoints can be controlled in two ways. A permanent connection (PC) is set up and maintained by a Network Management System (NMS) operating in the management plane. An operator manually provisions, tears down, and maintains these connections using management tools.

A switched connection (SC) is set up and maintained by signaling protocols in the control plane, such as RSVP-TE in GMPLS networks. These connections are established automatically by protocol messages sent between network elements.

A soft permanent connection (SPC) combines both: permanent connection segments at the network edges (under management plane control) and a switched connection segment in the core network (under control plane control). This hybrid approach can be useful when gradually introducing automated control to an existing network.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of cables: fully manual (you plug it in), fully automatic (the network sets it up), or mixed (edges are manual, the middle is automatic).

sections.title: Label Switched Paths and Resource Ownership
sections.content:
In GMPLS, a Label Switched Path (LSP) is a path through the network carrying data between two endpoints. An LSP has three aspects: a data plane path (the actual forwarding of packets), a management plane state (the NMS's configuration), and a control plane state (the control protocol's state). Different parts of the network might have different owners.

Resources used by a permanent connection are owned by the management plane. Resources used by a switched connection are owned by the control plane. An SPC divides resources: the management plane owns the edge segments and the control plane owns the core segment.

The conversion challenge is moving a working LSP from one ownership model to another without disrupting traffic. The management plane must initiate the change. When converting from PC to SC, the management plane tells each hop to switch from management control to protocol control. When converting from SC to PC, ownership reverts to the management plane and the control plane's state is removed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each cable has a list of settings in two places: the management computer's list, or the control computer's list. Conversion means rewriting that list across the whole path while data flows.

sections.title: Use Cases and Conversion Directions
sections.content:
PC-to-SC Conversion: A typical scenario is upgrading an existing network. All connections start under management plane control (PCs). As the network gradually introduces a GMPLS control plane, some connections can be converted to SC (fully automatic) or SPC (hybrid) control without interruption. This allows operators to extend control plane coverage without replacing the entire network.

SC-to-PC Conversion: If a connection running under control plane management encounters issues or if an operator needs to revert to manual control, converting from SC back to PC must also work without disruption. This acts as a back-out procedure if automation fails or if the operator wants to take direct control.

All intermediate conversions: PC to SPC, SPC to SC, SPC to PC, and SC to SPC must all be supported. The data plane path and all network resources stay exactly the same throughout.
sections.plainLanguage: You might start with all manual (PC), then make some cables automatic (SC). Or flip back. Or go partly automatic (SPC). All without stopping traffic.

sections.title: Requirements for Conversion
sections.content:
Data Plane Consistency: The data plane LSP path must not change. The same links and network resources must be used before, during, and after conversion. No rerouting or resource changes are permitted.

No Traffic Disruption: User traffic flowing over the LSP must not be interrupted or delayed. Additionally, the system must not generate alarms or notifications to end users or the NMS during conversion.

Ownership Transfer: It must be possible to transfer LSP ownership from the management plane to the control plane (required) and ideally in reverse (strongly desired). The management plane must initiate all such transfers.

State Synchronization: Before conversion is complete, the LSP state must be consistent across all nodes along the path. A two-phase commit approach, similar to database transactions, may be needed to ensure this and to enable rollback on failure.

Failure Recovery: If conversion fails partway through, the system must revert to the original state without affecting data plane traffic. The LSP must remain fully operational with its original ownership unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The path never changes, traffic never stops, the owner switches, all machines agree before it takes effect, and if it fails, we undo it.

sections.title: Security and Practical Deployment
sections.content:
Allowing control to be transferred introduces potential for service disruption through malicious intervention. Solutions must use existing security mechanisms from both the management plane and GMPLS control plane, particularly cryptographic security and role-based access control. Management plane protocols like NETCONF and SNMPv3 provide these capabilities and should be used.

Implementations may support policy controls to restrict which LSPs can be transferred. For instance, critical infrastructure might be locked to management plane control only, while best-effort traffic could move freely between planes.

This document is informational and sets out requirements for solution documents. It provides the foundation for protocol extensions and procedures that will enable carriers to evolve their networks gradually, supporting hybrid deployments and safe automation rollout without risk of traffic loss.
sections.plainLanguage: Access control keeps bad actors out. Policies let operators protect critical cables from being auto-controlled. Later documents will say how to actually do this.
